newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S. urges Japan not to stint on medical equipment.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges Japan not to stint on medical equipment.

text.p: The United States on Thursday urged Japan not to stint on the use of advanced medical equipment -- where Washington says U.S. firms are often at the leading edge -- in a misguided effort to cut health care costs.

"There is a general suspicion within the Japanese health care bureaucracy that innovative high technology and new products will add to the cost of the health care system in Japan," a U.S. official said after consultations here on Tokyo's proposals to reform its health care system.

"We frankly have some concern that as Japan looks for ways to cut costs in its health care system that it might again look at these types of products as an area where it might want to cut back," the official told reporters.

He added that this would be the wrong approach because advanced medical equipment can actually reduce costs in the long term, and because the root of Japan's high health care costs lies in other, systemic factors.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has made fiscal restructuring a top priority as Japan faces the ballooning cost of health care and other social welfare programmes due to its rapidly ageing population.
The official said the United States hopes to have "meaningful and frequent" opportunities to present its views as Japan debates how to provide the best health care within tight fiscal restraints.

Commenting on Japan's ongoing deregulation programme as it relates to medical equipment, the official said that the U.S. had seen some "modestly positive results" from three years of input into the process.
But he added, "there are still a number of areas where we think considerable further progress could and should be made".

The U.S. and Japan agreed earlier this month on an "enhanced deregulation initiative" to allow bilateral consultations on Japan's deregulation process in such areas as telecommunications, financial services and medical equipment.
But Hashimoto said explicitly at the time that Washington would not have an advisory or supervisory role over the process.
